reading.body:
Four of the five tools in this category are US-jurisdictioned, yet three of them explicitly carry GDPR or EU-candidate compliance notes, which means American vendors are already operating under European employment data rules whether or not their infrastructure sits in Europe.

The tools span the full hiring funnel, from initial candidate sourcing through screening, video interviewing, and scheduling, to longer-term talent lifecycle management. Every single entry carries a bias or DEI risk note. That is not an editorial choice, it is a structural feature of the domain: these systems make or shape high-stakes employment decisions at scale, and the training data and matching logic they rely on can encode historical workforce inequities directly into automated outcomes.

The compute angle here is indirect but real. Skills ontologies, video analysis, and large-scale candidate matching all run inference continuously against large populations, not in a single-query pattern. The data does not cover model size, inference volume, or energy draw for any of these platforms, so no claim about their grid footprint is warranted. What the data does establish is that HR AI is a category defined less by its hardware demands and more by its regulatory exposure, and that exposure is increasing, as the note on HireVue's regulatory scrutiny suggests, without specifying which regulators or what the outcomes were.
